opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest surprise was how far you could get with a relatively small amount of really high-quality data. When we started, we weren't sure whether training on browsing tasks would generalize beyond the specific kinds of questions we'd built datasets for. But once the model learned the core behaviors (searching, reading something, realizing it wasn't quite what it needed, refining the query, backtracking), those skills transferred surprisingly well to domains we hadn't explicitly targeted.

The other thing was how much the reasoning model itself mattered. Earlier attempts at browsing agents often got stuck: they'd do one search, grab the first plausible result, and stop. With a model trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning on these tasks, you see it actually reacting to what it finds. It'll notice that two sources disagree and go look for a third, or it'll realize halfway through that it misunderstood the question and change direction. That kind of adaptive planning wasn't something we hand-designed. It came out of the training.

And honestly, how people ended up using it surprised us too. We expected a lot of the use to be work research, like market analysis or literature reviews, and there is plenty of that. But people also use it for very personal things: researching a medical diagnosis for a family member, planning a big purchase, digging into a niche hobby. Seeing it be genuinely useful for things people care about deeply was really rewarding.

r001.rationale: The response says they were unsure whether browsing-task training would generalize, then describes the skills transferring surprisingly well to untargeted domains.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest surprise was how far end-to-end reinforcement learning took us on tasks that felt, honestly, kind of messy and open-ended. Browsing isn't like math or code, where there's a clean answer you can check. You're searching, opening pages, deciding what's relevant, backtracking when a source turns out to be useless, and then synthesizing all of that into something a person actually wants to read. Going in, I wasn't sure RL would generalize well to that kind of long-horizon, many-step environment.

And what we found was that the model got really good at the parts I expected to be hardest. It learned to be persistent in a way that's hard to prompt for. If the first few searches didn't turn up what it needed, it would reformulate, try different angles, dig into a PDF or a forum thread, and keep going for a long time. Early on we'd sometimes watch it take dozens of actions on a single query, and the trajectories actually made sense. It wasn't just flailing.

The other surprise was how much it transferred. We trained on a particular set of browsing tasks, but the capability showed up on things we hadn't explicitly targeted, like niche technical questions or finding very specific facts that were buried in obscure places. That generalization was a big signal for us that the approach was fundamentally sound, not just overfit to the training distribution.

And then the human side was surprising too. People started using it for things we didn't anticipate, like really personal research questions, shopping decisions, medical stuff where they wanted sources laid out. The fact that users were willing to wait several minutes for an answer was something we weren't sure about. It turns out if the output is good enough, people are pretty patient.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker was unsure reinforcement learning would generalize to messy, long-horizon browsing tasks, then describes being surprised by how well it worked.

astra-6.text: I think what surprised me most was how much you could get from training on the outcome, without prescribing exactly how the model should browse. You give it a question that requires research, and it starts learning useful strategies: searching in different ways, following up on a promising source, and going back when something doesn’t work. Those are behaviors you might otherwise try to build into a very elaborate workflow. Seeing them emerge through training—and come together into a much more persistent research process—was really exciting.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes being surprised by the results, but does not communicate prior confidence that training on browsing tasks would work.

sol-6.1.text: I think what surprised me was how much the model learned about the research process itself. Browsing sounds like a fairly narrow task—you search, you open a page, you find an answer. But when the answer takes a lot of steps to uncover, the model has to learn to recognize when a source isn’t useful, try a different approach, and keep track of what it still needs to figure out. Seeing those behaviors emerge from training was really interesting. It started to look less like following a fixed sequence of searches and more like working through a research problem.

r001.rationale: The response explains what was surprising about the learned research behaviors, but it does not state that there was prior confidence training on browsing tasks would work.
